title: Short Stuff: AAirpass
summary: Short Stuff episode on American Airlines' "AAirpass," a lifetime unlimited first-class travel program sold in the early 1980s to address airline financial troubles. Covers pricing changes over the years, the 28 buyers, famous holders, and how frequent flyers Jacques Room and Stephen Rothstein racked up huge mileage, resold companion passes, and were terminated by American, with lawsuits left unresolved.

segments.title: Naming the program and what it offered
segments.summary: The hosts open by deciding how to pronounce and spell the name, then explain the program: lifetime unlimited first-class travel, frequent flyer miles, and a lifetime Admirals Club membership, and note that it was expensive.

segments.title: Why airlines sold the pass and who bought it
segments.summary: American Airlines was struggling after the 1970s and early 1980s, with revenue down and a $76 million loss in 1980 following the Deregulation Act of 1978. Selling prepaid lifetime passes beat borrowing at high interest rates. Willie Mays, Mark Cuban and Michael Dell were among buyers, and 28 people bought in.

segments.title: Pricing changes over time
segments.summary: The pass started at $250,000 with a $150,000 companion pass, rose to $600,000 with the companion, then $1.01 million in 1993, and in 2004 was offered in a Neiman Marcus catalog at $3 million plus $2 million for a companion. No one is known to have bought the final offer.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts announce a break before discussing the heavy-flying buyers.

segments.title: Jacques Room and Stephen Rothstein's heavy travel
segments.summary: Jacques Room and Stephen Rothstein, a Bear Stearns investment banker, became prominent heavy users. They traveled tens of millions of miles, including flights for trivial errands, and the hosts describe Room's habit of flying to pick up his father-in-law to babysit and flying to London for motorcycle tires.

segments.title: Companion pass resale and American's response
segments.summary: The men sold or gave away companion passes to strangers, and Room reportedly earned $100,000 from one couple for travel to Europe. Rules did not explicitly forbid this in the original contract. American formed a Revenue Integrity Team, terminated both passes, and lawsuits followed; the parent company later filed for bankruptcy and the suits remain unresolved.

segments.title: Family perspective and closing thoughts
segments.summary: Caroline Rothstein is quoted saying her father was treated unfairly and lived to travel. The hosts discuss the bitterness of losing the pass and suggest the men may have been targeted because they were the least wealthy holders.

segments.title: Sign-off and sources
segments.summary: The hosts recommend reading articles by Zachary Crockett, Ken Benzinger of the Los Angeles Times, and Caroline Rothstein, then sign off.
